claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- mice had consistently reduced body weight compared to heterozygous Nrn1+/-, WT (Nrn1+/+) mice.
claims.source: In the first evaluation of the Nrn1-/- colony, Nrn1-/- mice had consistently reduced body weight compared to heterozygous Nrn1+/-, WT (Nrn1+/+) mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: The lymphoid tissues of Nrn1-/- mice were comparable to their Nrn1+/-, WT counterparts except for a slight reduction in cell number that was observed in the spleens of Nrn1-/- mice.
claims.source: The lymphoid tissues of Nrn1-/- mice were comparable to their Nrn1+/-, WT counterparts except for a slight reduction in cell number that was observed in the spleens of Nrn1-/- mice, likely due to their smaller size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: Analysis of thymocytes revealed no defect in T cell development in Nrn1-/- mice.
claims.source: Analysis of thymocytes revealed no defect in T cell development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: A flow cytometric survey of the major immune cell populations in the peripheral lymphoid tissue revealed similar proportions of CD4, CD8 T cells, B cells, monocytes and dendritic cells (DCs) in Nrn1-/-, Nrn1+/-, WT mice.
claims.source: a flow cytometric survey of the major immune cell populations in the peripheral lymphoid tissue of these mice revealed similar proportions of CD4, CD8 T cells, B cells, monocytes and dendritic cells (DCs; Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: No differences were found between the proportions of anergic and Treg cells in Nrn1-/-, Nrn1+/-, WT mice.
claims.source: Similarly, no differences were found between the proportions of anergic and Treg cells in Nrn1-/-, Nrn1+/-, WT mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, F)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E, F.

claims.claim: Histopathology assessment of lung, heart, liver, kidney, intestine, and spleen harvested from 13 months old Nrn1-/- and Nrn1+/- did not reveal any evidence of autoimmunity.
claims.source: Additionally, histopathology assessment of lung, heart, liver, kidney, intestine, and spleen harvested from 13 months old Nrn1-/- and Nrn1+/- did not reveal any evidence of autoimmunity (data not shown).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated based on histopathology assessment data.

claims.claim: The proportion and number of OTII cells increased in the Nrn1-/-_OTII compared to the ctrl_OTII hosts on day 13 after cell transfer.
claims.source: On day 13 after cell transfer, the proportion and number of OTII cells increased in the Nrn1-/-_OTII compared to the ctrl_OTII hosts (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/-_OTII cells produced increased IL2 than ctrl_OTII upon restimulation.
claims.source: Moreover, Nrn1-/-_OTII cells produced increased IL2 than ctrl_OTII upon restimulation (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: The proportion of FOXP3+ pTreg among Nrn1-/-_OTII was significantly reduced.
claims.source: Consistent with reduced anergy induction, the proportion of FOXP3+ pTreg among Nrn1-/-_OTII was significantly reduced (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claims.claim: The gene set on T cell anergy was enriched in ctrl relative to Nrn1-/-_OTII cells.
claims.source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that the gene set on T cell anergy was enriched in ctrl relative to Nrn1-/-_OTII cells (Figure 1I; Safford et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1I and citation to published gene set.

claims.claim: The Treg signature gene set was prominently reduced in Nrn1-/-_OTII cells relative to the ctrl.
claims.source: Also, consistent with the decreased transdifferentiation to FOXP3+ cells, the Treg signature gene set was prominently reduced in Nrn1-/-_OTII cells relative to the ctrl (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- CD4+ cells showed reduced T cell activation, as evidenced by reduced CellTrace violet dye (CTV) dilution, activation marker expression, and Ca++ entry after TCR stimulation.
claims.source: Nrn1-/- CD4+ cells showed reduced T cell activation, as evidenced by reduced CellTrace violet dye (CTV) dilution, activation marker expression, and Ca++ entry after TCR stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B, C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B, C.

claims.claim: Similar proportions of FOXP3+ cells were observed in Nrn1-/- and ctrl cells under the iTreg culture condition.
claims.source: Similar proportions of FOXP3+ cells were observed in Nrn1-/- and ctrl cells under the iTreg culture condition (Figure 2A)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Reduced live cells over time were found in Nrn1-/- iTreg compared to the ctrl after restimulation with anti-CD3.
claims.source: To examine the capacity of iTreg expansion, Nrn1-/- and ctrl iTreg cells were restimulated with anti-CD3, and we found reduced live cells over time in Nrn1-/- iTreg compared to the ctrl (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The reduced live cell number in Nrn1-/- iTreg was accompanied by reduced Ki67 expression.
claims.source: The reduced live cell number in Nrn1-/- was accompanied by reduced Ki67 expression (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- iTregs retained a higher proportion of FOXP3+ cells 3 days after restimulation.
claims.source: Although Nrn1-/- iTregs retained a higher proportion of FOXP3+ cells 3 days after restimulation, however, when taking into account the total number of live cells, the actual number of live FOXP3+ cells was reduced in Nrn1-/- (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The actual number of live FOXP3+ cells was reduced in Nrn1-/- iTreg 3 days after restimulation.
claims.source: Although Nrn1-/- iTregs retained a higher proportion of FOXP3+ cells 3 days after restimulation, however, when taking into account the total number of live cells, the actual number of live FOXP3+ cells was reduced in Nrn1-/- (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- nTreg cells retained a higher FOXP3+ cell proportion and reduced Ki67 expression compared to the ctrl at day 7 post transfer.
claims.source: Although the CD45.1-CD45.2+ Nrn1-/- and ctrl cell proportions were not significantly different among hosts splenocytes at day 7 post transfer (Figure 2F), Nrn1-/- cells retained a higher FOXP3+ cell proportion and reduced Ki67 expression comparing to the ctrl (Figure 2G and H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- Tregs showed reduced suppression toward CD45.1+ responder cells, evidenced by increased CD45.1+ proportion and cell number in host splenocytes.
claims.source: Nrn1-/- Tregs also showed reduced suppression toward CD45.1+ responder cells, evidenced by increased CD45.1+ proportion and cell number in host splenocytes (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Tumors grew much slower in Nrn1-/- Treg recipients than those reconstituted with ctrl Tregs.
claims.source: Tumors grew much slower in Nrn1-/- Treg recipients than those reconstituted with ctrl Tregs (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: The number of CD45.1+ cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes and spleens increased significantly in Nrn1-/- Treg hosts compared to the ctrl group.
claims.source: Moreover, the number of CD45.1+ cells in tumor-draining lymph nodes and spleens increased significantly in Nrn1-/- Treg hosts compared to the ctrl group (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: The CD45.1+ responder cell proportion among tumor lymphocyte infiltrates (TILs) was increased in Nrn1-/- Treg hosts.
claims.source: Consistently, the CD45.1+ responder cell proportion among tumor lymphocyte infiltrates (TILs) was also increased (Figure 2L)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L.

claims.claim: An increased proportion of IFNγ + cells among CD8 TILs was observed from Nrn1-/- Treg hosts.
claims.source: accompanied by an increased proportion of IFNγ + cells among CD8 TILs from Nrn1-/- Treg hosts (Figure 2M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2M.

claims.claim: Three clusters were enriched in resting Nrn1-/- iTreg identified by GSEA on gene ontology database and clustering of enriched gene sets by Cytoscape.
claims.source: GSEA on gene ontology database and clustering of enriched gene sets by Cytoscape identified three clusters enriched in resting Nrn1-/- iTreg (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1; Shannon et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3A and citations to analysis methods.

claims.claim: The 'neurotransmitter involved in membrane potential (MP)' and 'sodium transport' clusters involved gene sets on the ion transport and cell MP regulation.
claims.source: The 'neurotransmitter involved in membrane potential (MP)' and 'sodium transport' clusters involved gene sets on the ion transport and cell MP regulation (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The 'Neurotransmitter receptor activity involved in regulation of postsynaptic membrane potential' gene set was significantly enriched under resting and activation conditions in Nrn1-/- cells.
claims.source: The 'Neurotransmitter receptor activity involved in regulation of postsynaptic membrane potential' gene set was significantly enriched under resting and activation conditions In Nrn1-/- cells (Figure 3C and D; Figure 3—source data 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3C and D.

claims.claim: The AMPAR subunits Gria2 and Gria3 showed increased expression in Nrn1-/- cells.
claims.source: The α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits Gria2 and Gria3 are the major components of this gene set and showed increased expression in Nrn1-/- cells (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Nrn1 has been reported as an accessory protein for AMPAR.
claims.source: Nrn1 has been reported as an accessory protein for AMPAR (Pandya et al., 2018; Schwenk et al., 2012; Subramanian et al., 2019)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- iTreg exhibits significant hyperpolarization under both resting and activation conditions compared to ctrl iTreg cells.
claims.source: Compared to ctrl iTreg cells, Nrn1-/- exhibits significant hyperpolarization under both resting and activation conditions (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane potential measurement data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The 'MF_metal ion transmembrane transporter activity' gene set was significantly enriched and showed a different expression pattern in Nrn1-/- iTregs.
claims.source: Consistent with the MP change, the 'MF_metal ion transmembrane transporter activity' gene set, which contains 436 ion channel related genes, was significantly enriched and showed a different expression pattern in Nrn1-/- iTregs (Figure 3F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3F and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Differential AA transporter gene expression was found between Nrn1-/- and ctrl iTregs.
claims.source: we surveyed AA transport-related gene expression using the 'Amino acid transmembrane transporter activity' gene set and found differential AA transporter gene expression between Nrn1-/- and ctrl iTregs (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The AA-induced cellular MP change was reduced in Nrn1-/- iTreg compared to the ctrl.
claims.source: The AA-induced cellular MP change was reduced in Nrn1-/- compared to the ctrl, reflective of differential AA transporter expression patterns (Figure 3H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane potential measurement data shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: Reduced phosphorylation of mTOR and S6 was found in activated Nrn1-/- iTreg cells.
claims.source: We examined mTORC1 activation at the protein level by evaluating mTOR and S6 phosphorylation via flow cytometry. We found reduced phosphorylation of mTOR and S6 in activated Nrn1-/- iTreg cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The degree of mTOR and S6 phosphorylation change after nutrient sensing was significantly less in Nrn1-/- iTreg than in the ctrl.
claims.source: While adding the medium with nutrients clearly increased the mTOR and S6 phosphorylation, the degree of change was significantly less in Nrn1-/- than in the ctrl (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by nutrient sensing assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- iTreg cells showed reduced expression of glycolysis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation related gene sets under both resting and activating conditions.
claims.source: Moreover, Nrn1-/- cells also showed reduced expression of glycolysis, fatty acid metabolism, and oxidative phosphorylation related gene sets under both resting and activating conditions (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Reduced glycolysis was confirmed among Nrn1-/- iTreg cells by seahorse assay.
claims.source: we performed the seahorse assay and confirmed reduced glycolysis among Nrn1-/- cells (Figure 3K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seahorse assay data shown in Figure 3K.

claims.claim: A similar oxygen consumption rate (OCR) was observed between Nrn1-/- and ctrl iTreg cells.
claims.source: Examination of mitochondrial bioenergetic function revealed a similar oxygen consumption rate (OCR) between Nrn1-/- and ctrl cells (Figure 3K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seahorse assay data shown in Figure 3K.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- naïve CD4 T cells showed similar resting MP and AA-induced MP changes compared to the ctrl cells.
claims.source: The Nrn1-/- naïve CD4 T cells showed similar resting MP and AA-induced MP changes compared to the ctrl cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane potential measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, B.

claims.claim: Comparable glycolysis and mitochondrial bioenergetic function were observed between Nrn1-/- naïve CD4 T cells and the ctrl.
claims.source: We also observed comparable glycolysis and mitochondrial bioenergetic function between Nrn1-/- naïve CD4 T cells and the ctrl (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seahorse assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: WT iTreg cells differentiated in the presence of Nrn1 antibody exhibit reduced resting MP, similar to Nrn1-/- cells.
claims.source: WT iTreg cells differentiated in the presence of Nrn1 antibody exhibit reduced resting MP, similar to Nrn1-/- cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane potential measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claims.claim: WT iTreg cells differentiated under NRN1 antibody blockade showed a similar phenotype as Nrn1-/- cells upon restimulation, with reduced live cell number, reduced Ki67 expression, and increased FOXP3+ cell proportion among live cells.
claims.source: Moreover, upon restimulation, WT iTreg cells differentiated under NRN1 antibody blockade showed a similar phenotype as Nrn1-/- cells, with reduced live cell number, reduced Ki67 expression, and increased FOXP3+ cell proportion among live cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E, F.

claims.claim: Nrn1 deficient CD4 Te cells showed increased Ki67 expression, associated with increased cytokine TNFa, Il2, and IFNγ expression upon restimulation.
claims.source: Nrn1 deficient CD4 Te cells showed increased Ki67 expression, associated with increased cytokine TNFa, Il2, and IFNγ expression upon restimulation (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Accelerated weight loss was observed in Nrn1-/-_FDG mice upon administration of DT.
claims.source: Upon administration of DT, we observed accelerated weight loss in Nrn1-/-_FDG mice, reflecting enhanced autoimmune inflammation (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: A significant increase in Ki67 expression and inflammatory cytokine TNFa, IL2, and IFNγ expression among Nrn1-/- CD4 cells was observed on day 6 post DT treatment.
claims.source: Examination of T cell response revealed a significant increase in Ki67 expression and inflammatory cytokine TNFa, IL2, and IFNγ expression among Nrn1-/- CD4 cells on day 6 post DT treatment (Figure 4D)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The proportion of FOXP3+ cells was very low on day 6 post DT treatment and comparable between Nrn1-/- and the ctrl.
claims.source: The proportion of FOXP3+ cells was very low on day 6 post DT treatment and comparable between Nrn1-/- and the ctrl (Figure 4E)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: A cluster of gene sets on 'membrane repolarization' was identified in Nrn1-/- Te cells by GSEA and Cytoscape analysis.
claims.source: GSEA and Cytoscape analysis identified a cluster of gene sets on 'membrane repolarization', suggesting that Nrn1 may also be involved in the regulation of MP under Te context (Figure 4F, Figure 4—source data 1; Shannon et al., 2003; Subramanian et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4F and citations to analysis methods.

claims.claim: The 'membrane_repolarization' gene set was enriched in Nrn1-/- Te cells.
claims.source: While the 'membrane_repolarization' gene set was enriched in Nrn1-/- (Figure 4G)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The AMPAR subunit Gria3 expression was elevated in Nrn1-/- Te cells.
claims.source: the 'Neurotransmitter receptor activity involved in regulation of postsynaptic membrane potential' gene set was no longer enriched, but the AMPAR subunit Gria3 expression was still elevated in Nrn1-/- Te cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MP in Te cells was comparable between Nrn1-/- and ctrl.
claims.source: Although MP in Te cells was comparable between Nrn1-/- and ctrl (Figure 4H)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane potential measurement data shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: The 'MF_metal ion transmembrane transporter activity' gene set was significantly enriched in Nrn1-/- Te cells with different gene expression patterns.
claims.source: the 'MF_metal ion transmembrane transporter activity' gene set was significantly enriched in Nrn1-/- with different gene expression patterns (Figure 4I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The 'Amino acid transmembrane transporter activity' gene set was significantly enriched in Nrn1-/- Te cells than the ctrl.
claims.source: Examination of nutrient transporters revealed that the 'Amino acid transmembrane transporter activity' gene set was significantly enriched in Nrn1-/- cells than the ctrl (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: AA entry caused enhanced MP change among Nrn1-/- Te than the ctrl.
claims.source: AA entry caused enhanced MP change among Nrn1-/- Te than the ctrl, in contrast with the finding under iTreg cell context (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by membrane potential measurement data shown in Figure 4K.

claims.claim: Enhanced mTOR and S6 phosphorylation was found in Nrn1-/- Te cells.
claims.source: Along with the enrichment of ion channel and nutrient transporter genes (Figure 4I and J), we found enhanced mTOR and S6 phosphorylation in Nrn1-/- Te cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- Te showed increased mTOR and S6 phosphorylation after sensing ions and nutrients in RPMI medium.
claims.source: Nrn1-/- Te showed increased mTOR and S6 phosphorylation after sensing ions and nutrients in RPMI medium (Figure 4L)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by nutrient sensing assay data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: Nrn1-/- Te cells showed enrichment of gene sets on glycolysis and proliferation.
claims.source: Along with increased mTORC1 signaling, Nrn1-/- Te cells also showed enrichment of gene sets on glycolysis and proliferation (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4M.

claims.claim: Increased glycolysis was confirmed in Nrn1-/- Te cells by seahorse assay, while the OCR remained comparable between Nrn1-/- and ctrl.
claims.source: Evaluation of metabolic changes by seahorse confirmed increased glycolysis in Nrn1-/- cells, while the OCR remained comparable between Nrn1-/- and ctrl (Figure 4N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by seahorse assay data shown in Figure 4N.

claims.claim: The incidence and time to EAE onset in Nrn1-/- mice were comparable to the ctrl mice.
claims.source: Upon EAE induction, the incidence and time to EAE onset in Nrn1-/- mice were comparable to the ctrl mice, but the severity, disease persistence, and body weight loss were increased in Nrn1-/- mice (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EAE disease monitoring data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The severity, disease persistence, and body weight loss were increased in Nrn1-/- mice upon EAE induction.
claims.source: Upon EAE induction, the incidence and time to EAE onset in Nrn1-/- mice were comparable to the ctrl mice, but the severity, disease persistence, and body weight loss were increased in Nrn1-/- mice (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EAE disease monitoring data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Exacerbated EAE was associated with significantly increased CD45+ cell infiltrates in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord.
claims.source: Exacerbated EAE was associated with significantly increased CD45+ cell infiltrates, increased CD4+ cell number, increased proportion of MOG-specific CD4 cells, and reduced proportion of FOXP3+ CD4 cells in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord (Figure 5B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Exacerbated EAE was associated with increased CD4+ cell number in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord.
claims.source: Exacerbated EAE was associated with significantly increased CD45+ cell infiltrates, increased CD4+ cell number, increased proportion of MOG-specific CD4 cells, and reduced proportion of FOXP3+ CD4 cells in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord (Figure 5B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Exacerbated EAE was associated with increased proportion of MOG-specific CD4 cells in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord.
claims.source: Exacerbated EAE was associated with significantly increased CD45+ cell infiltrates, increased CD4+ cell number, increased proportion of MOG-specific CD4 cells, and reduced proportion of FOXP3+ CD4 cells in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord (Figure 5B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by tetramer staining data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Exacerbated EAE was associated with reduced proportion of FOXP3+ CD4 cells in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord.
claims.source: Exacerbated EAE was associated with significantly increased CD45+ cell infiltrates, increased CD4+ cell number, increased proportion of MOG-specific CD4 cells, and reduced proportion of FOXP3+ CD4 cells in the Nrn1-/- spinal cord (Figure 5B–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Increased proportions of IFNγ+ and IL17+ CD4 cells were observed in Nrn1-/- mice remaining in the draining lymph node compared to the ctrl mice.
claims.source: Moreover, we also observed increased proportions of IFNγ+ and IL17+ CD4 cells in Nrn1-/- mice remaining in the draining lymph node compared to the ctrl mice (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: Peripheral T cell tolerance is important in restricting autoimmunity and minimizing collateral damage during active immune reactions.
claims.source: Peripheral T cell tolerance is important in restricting autoimmunity and minimizing collateral damage during active immune reactions and is achieved via diverse mechanisms, including T cell anergy, regulatory T (Treg) cell mediated suppression, and effector T (Te) cell exhaustion or deletion (ElTanbouly and Noelle, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claims.claim: Peripheral T cell tolerance is achieved via diverse mechanisms, including T cell anergy, regulatory T (Treg) cell mediated suppression, and effector T (Te) cell exhaustion or deletion.
claims.source: Peripheral T cell tolerance is important in restricting autoimmunity and minimizing collateral damage during active immune reactions and is achieved via diverse mechanisms, including T cell anergy, regulatory T (Treg) cell mediated suppression, and effector T (Te) cell exhaustion or deletion (ElTanbouly and Noelle, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claims.claim: T cell anergy is associated with reduced glycolysis.
claims.source: For example, T cell anergy is associated with reduced glycolysis, whereas activated T effector cells exhibit increased glycolysis (Buck et al., 2017; Geltink et al., 2018; Peng and Li, 2023; Zheng et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Activated T effector cells exhibit increased glycolysis.
claims.source: For example, T cell anergy is associated with reduced glycolysis, whereas activated T effector cells exhibit increased glycolysis (Buck et al., 2017; Geltink et al., 2018; Peng and Li, 2023; Zheng et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Cellular metabolic states depend on electrolyte and nutrient uptake from the microenvironment.
claims.source: Cellular metabolic states depend on electrolyte and nutrient uptake from the microenvironment (Chapman and Chi, 2022; Olenchock et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Ion channels and nutrient transporters can integrate environmental nutrient changes and affect the cellular metabolic choices and impact the T cell functional outcome.
claims.source: Ion channels and nutrient transporters, which can integrate environmental nutrient changes, affect the cellular metabolic choices and impact the T cell functional outcome (Babst, 2020; Bohmwald et al., 2021; Ramirez et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Anergic CD4 Tconv cells can transdifferentiate into FOXP3+ pTreg cells in vivo.
claims.source: Anergic CD4 Tconv cells can transdifferentiate into FOXP3+ pTreg cells in vivo (Kaleka and Daniel L Mueller, 2017; Kalekar et al., 2016; Kuczma et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Anergic T cells are developed after encountering antigen, passing through a brief effector stage, and reaching an anergic state.
claims.source: Anergic T cells are developed after encountering antigen, passing through a brief effector stage, and reaching an anergic state (Chappert and Schwartz, 2010; Huang et al., 2003; Silva Morales and Mueller, 2018; Zha et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Anergic T cells are characterized by inhibition of proliferation and compromised effector cytokines such as IL2 production.
claims.source: Anergic T cells are characterized by inhibition of proliferation and compromised effector cytokines such as IL2 production (Choi and Schwartz, 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claims.claim: Treg cells are not stable and are prone to losing FOXP3 expression after extended proliferation.
claims.source: Treg cells are not stable and are prone to losing FOXP3 expression after extended proliferation (Feng et al., 2014; Floess et al., 2007; Li et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: MP is the difference in electric charge between the interior and the exterior of the cell membrane.
claims.source: MP is the difference in electric charge between the interior and the exterior of the cell membrane (Abdul Kadir et al., 2018; Blackiston et al., 2009; Ma et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: Ion channels and transporters for Na+ and other ions such as K+, Cl- et al. maintain the ion balance and contribute to cell MP.
claims.source: Ion channels and transporters for Na+ and other ions such as K+, Cl- et al. maintain the ion balance and contribute to cell MP (Blackiston et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claims.claim: MP change can impact cell plasma membrane lipid dynamics and affect receptor kinase activity.
claims.source: MP change can impact cell plasma membrane lipid dynamics and affect receptor kinase activity (Zhou et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claims.claim: Electrolytes and AAs entry are critical regulators of mTORC1 activation and T cell metabolism.
claims.source: Electrolytes and AAs entry are critical regulators of mTORC1 activation and T cell metabolism (Liu and Sabatini, 2020; Saravia et al., 2020; Sinclair et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published work.

claims.claim: mTORC1 is an important regulator of aerobic glycolysis.
claims.source: Since previous work has identified mTORC1 to be an important regulator of aerobic glycolysis and given that our GSEA data suggested changes in glycolysis (Figure 3J; Salmond, 2018)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published work.

claims.claim: CD4+ T cells may pass through an effector stage after activation before reaching an anergic state.
claims.source: CD4+ T cells may pass through an effector stage after activation before reaching an anergic state (Adler et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2004; Huang et al., 2003; Opejin et al., 2020).

results.result: Nrn1 is a highly conserved neurotrophic factor that plays multiple roles in neural development and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 are well-supported by citations to established literature describing Nrn1's discovery, conservation, and neuronal functions. These are background claims establishing prior knowledge about Nrn1.

results.result: Nrn1 expression has been previously reported in various immune cell populations associated with tolerance, including Tregs, anergic T cells, and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 are supported by multiple citations to published studies documenting Nrn1 expression in immune contexts. These establish the rationale for investigating Nrn1's role in T cell tolerance.

results.result: Nrn1 expression is significantly elevated in anergic T cells, Tregs, tumor-infiltrating T cells, and activated T cells compared to naive or peripheral blood T cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C15 are supported by qRT-PCR, western blot, and flow cytometry data (Figures 1A-D and supplements). The data consistently show elevated Nrn1 expression in tolerance-associated T cell populations across multiple experimental systems.

results.result: Nrn1-/- mice show reduced body weight but have largely normal immune system development and composition under steady-state conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C21 are supported by comprehensive phenotypic characterization data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The data show minor differences (body weight, spleen cellularity) but no major developmental defects or spontaneous autoimmunity, establishing that Nrn1 deficiency does not cause baseline immune dysfunction.

results.result: Nrn1 deficiency impairs T cell anergy induction in vivo, as evidenced by increased OTII cell expansion, enhanced IL2 production, reduced pTreg generation, and decreased expression of anergy and Treg signature genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are supported by data from the peptide-induced anergy model (Figure 1F-J), including cell counts, cytokine production, FOXP3+ cell proportions, and RNASeq/GSEA analysis. Claim C27 shows reduced early activation, ruling out hyperactivation as the cause. The data collectively demonstrate defective anergy development in Nrn1-/- cells.

results.result: Nrn1-/- iTregs show normal FOXP3+ differentiation but impaired expansion upon restimulation, with reduced live cell numbers, decreased Ki67 expression, and ultimately fewer total FOXP3+ cells despite higher proportions.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are supported by in vitro iTreg differentiation and restimulation experiments (Figure 2A-D). The data distinguish between differentiation (normal) and expansion (impaired) defects, with appropriate controls and multiple readouts.

results.result: Nrn1-/- nTregs exhibit reduced suppressive function in vivo, as demonstrated by decreased suppression of responder cell expansion and enhanced anti-tumor immunity in adoptive transfer experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are supported by in vivo Treg suppression assays (Figure 2E-M). The data show consistent phenotypes across multiple readouts: reduced Ki67, increased responder cell expansion, slower tumor growth, and enhanced CD8+ T cell function. The experimental design appropriately tests Treg suppressive capacity.

results.result: Nrn1-/- iTregs show enrichment of ion channel and membrane potential-related gene sets, including AMPAR subunits, and exhibit significant hyperpolarization compared to control cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42, C44-C45 are supported by RNASeq/GSEA analysis and membrane potential measurements (Figure 3A-F). The data identify specific gene sets and validate the functional consequence (hyperpolarization) using FLIPR dye. The connection between gene expression and cellular phenotype is demonstrated.

results.result: Nrn1-/- iTregs show altered amino acid transporter expression, reduced amino acid-induced membrane potential changes, decreased mTORC1 signaling, and reduced glycolysis without changes in oxidative phosphorylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 are supported by RNASeq, membrane potential assays, flow cytometry for phospho-proteins, and seahorse metabolic assays (Figure 3G-K). The data establish a mechanistic link from nutrient transporter expression through mTORC1 signaling to metabolic changes.

results.result: Nrn1-/- naive CD4 T cells show normal membrane potential and metabolic function, indicating that changes in iTregs are not due to developmental defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by membrane potential and seahorse assays on naive T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C). This control experiment is critical for ruling out developmental/structural explanations for the iTreg phenotype.

results.result: Antibody blockade of Nrn1 during WT iTreg differentiation recapitulates the Nrn1-/- phenotype, demonstrating that functional Nrn1 activity rather than developmental changes is responsible for the observed effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are supported by antibody blocking experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-F). This is a critical control showing that acute Nrn1 blockade phenocopies genetic deletion, supporting a functional rather than developmental role.

results.result: Nrn1-/- effector T cells show enhanced proliferation and inflammatory cytokine production in vitro and exacerbated autoimmune inflammation in vivo following Treg depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by in vitro Te cell differentiation and in vivo Treg depletion experiments (Figure 4A-E). The data show consistent enhancement of Te cell responses across multiple readouts, with appropriate controls showing comparable FOXP3+ depletion.

results.result: Nrn1-/- Te cells show enrichment of membrane repolarization and ion channel gene sets, with elevated Gria3 expression, but comparable overall membrane potential to controls despite differential ion channel expression patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 are supported by RNASeq/GSEA and membrane potential measurements (Figure 4F-I). The data show that Nrn1 affects ion channel expression in Te cells differently than in iTregs, with distinct functional consequences on membrane potential.

results.result: Nrn1-/- Te cells show enrichment of amino acid transporter genes, enhanced amino acid-induced membrane potential changes, increased mTORC1 signaling, and elevated glycolysis—opposite to the effects in iTregs.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by RNASeq, membrane potential assays, phospho-protein flow cytometry, and seahorse assays (Figure 4J-N). The data demonstrate cell-context-dependent effects of Nrn1, with Te cells showing opposite metabolic changes compared to iTregs.

results.result: Nrn1-/- mice develop more severe EAE with increased disease persistence, enhanced immune cell infiltration into the CNS, increased MOG-specific CD4+ cells, reduced Treg proportions, and elevated inflammatory cytokine production.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C78 are supported by comprehensive EAE disease monitoring and immunological analysis (Figure 5A-F). The data show consistent exacerbation across clinical and immunological parameters, demonstrating the physiological relevance of Nrn1 in autoimmune disease.

results.result: Background knowledge claims establishing the conceptual framework for T cell tolerance, metabolism, membrane potential, ion channels, nutrient transporters, and Nrn1's known molecular interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C108 are supported by citations to published literature. These establish the scientific context and rationale for the study, including mechanisms of tolerance, metabolic regulation, bioelectric control, and Nrn1's known functions.

results.result: Nrn1 modulates T cell tolerance and immunity in a cell-context-dependent manner, promoting Treg expansion and suppression while dampening effector T cell inflammatory responses, thereby impacting autoimmune disease outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C116 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all experimental findings. These are well-supported by the comprehensive data showing opposite effects in Tregs (reduced expansion/suppression) versus Te cells (enhanced inflammation) and the physiological consequences in EAE. The claims are appropriately qualified as being demonstrated in mice.

results.result: Nrn1 expression is elevated in anergic T cells (Ta), Treg cells (nTreg and iTreg), and tumor-associated T cells in both mouse and human samples, and is induced upon CD4+ T cell activation. This expression pattern was characterized by qRT-PCR, western blot, and flow cytometry using an NRN1-specific monoclonal antibody.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 requests confirmation of the anti-Nrn1 mAb specificity by FACS using Nrn1 KO mice and suggests adding FACS results to Figures 1A-C for single-cell quantitative data. The characterization is described as 'comprehensive and convincing' by Reviewer 3, but the lack of antibody validation in knockout mice creates uncertainty about the specificity of detection.

results.result: Nrn1-/- mice show reduced body weight but otherwise normal immune system development at homeostasis, with comparable lymphoid tissue cellularity, T cell development, immune cell populations, anergic and Treg cell proportions, and no evidence of spontaneous autoimmunity.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern that Nrn1+/- and Nrn1+/+ cells are used indiscriminately as controls based on homeostatic similarity, but may have different phenotypes under activation or inflammatory conditions. The reviewer requests discrimination of these genotypes or demonstration that both have the same phenotype under stress conditions, which undermines confidence in the baseline characterization.

results.result: In an in vivo anergy induction model using OTII T cells transferred to C3-HA hosts, Nrn1-/- OTII cells showed reduced anergy induction with increased cell numbers, increased IL2 production, reduced FOXP3+ pTreg differentiation, and reduced anergy and Treg gene set signatures compared to control.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states that 'the authors assume that this immunization protocol induces anergic cells, but they provide no experimental evidence for this' and requests demonstration that T cells are indeed anergic, especially OVA-specific cells. The reviewer notes that 'the lack of IL-2 production by Ctrl cells could be explained by the presence of fewer OVA-specific cells, rather than by an anergic status,' indicating the conclusions are not adequately supported.

results.result: Nrn1-/- CD4+ cells showed reduced T cell activation as measured by CellTrace violet dilution, activation marker expression, and calcium entry after TCR stimulation.
results.evaluation: This finding is not specifically critiqued by reviewers and is consistent with the overall narrative. Reviewer 3 notes that 'naive cells lacking Nrn1 expression show normal electrical and metabolic behaviors,' which is consistent with context-dependent effects of Nrn1 deletion.

results.result: Nrn1-/- iTreg cells show normal initial FOXP3+ differentiation but reduced expansion capacity upon restimulation, with decreased live cell numbers, reduced Ki67 expression, and ultimately fewer total FOXP3+ cells despite retaining higher FOXP3+ proportions.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 states that 'the use of iTregs to try to understand what is happening in vivo is problematic. iTregs are cells that have probably no equivalent in vivo, and so may have no physiological relevance.' The reviewer suggests generating data with purified nTreg instead, questioning the biological relevance of these findings.

results.result: In an in vivo tumor model, Nrn1-/- nTreg cells showed reduced suppressive function with slower tumor growth, increased responder cell numbers in lymphoid organs and tumors, and increased IFNγ+ CD8 T cells in tumor infiltrates.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a critical concern that 'the % of Foxp3+ among CD45.2 nTreg cells fell to 5-15% of CD4+ cells' and notes uncertainty about whether this reflects Treg instability or contaminating Tconv expansion. The reviewer states 'it is very likely that there are Tconv contaminants that would be Nrn1-/- in the group transferred with Nrn1-/- "nTreg", the higher tumor rejection could be due to an overactivation of Nrn1-/- Tconvs (rather than a defect in Nrn1-/- Treg function),' directly challenging the interpretation.

results.result: Nrn1-/- iTreg cells show enrichment of gene sets related to neurotransmitter receptors, ion channels, and amino acid transporters, with increased expression of AMPAR subunits Gria2 and Gria3, hyperpolarized membrane potential, and reduced amino acid-induced membrane potential changes.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'data shown here provide evidence for alterations in the electrical and metabolic state of iTreg and Teff cells when the Nrn1 gene is deleted' but emphasizes that 'it remains unclear how Nrn1 reinforces the membrane potential and facilitates aerobic glycolysis during and after iTreg differentiation.' Reviewer 2's concern about iTreg physiological relevance also applies here. The data are present but mechanistic understanding is lacking.

results.result: Nrn1-/- iTreg cells show reduced mTOR and S6 phosphorylation, reduced nutrient sensing capacity, reduced expression of glycolysis and metabolic gene sets, and confirmed reduced glycolysis by seahorse assay, while maintaining similar oxygen consumption rates.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes the metabolic alterations but states 'it remains unclear how Nrn1 reinforces the membrane potential and facilitates aerobic glycolysis during and after iTreg differentiation.' Reviewer 2's concerns about iTreg relevance and the small number of biological replicates (especially 'RNAseq bulk data are based on biological duplicates') undermine confidence in these findings.

results.result: Nrn1-/- naïve CD4 T cells show normal resting membrane potential, amino acid-induced membrane potential changes, and comparable glycolysis and mitochondrial function compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'importantly, naive cells lacking Nrn1 expression show normal electrical and metabolic behaviors,' affirming this finding as an important control demonstrating context-dependent effects of Nrn1.

results.result: WT iTreg cells differentiated in the presence of anti-Nrn1 antibody phenocopy Nrn1-/- cells with reduced membrane potential, reduced live cell numbers, reduced Ki67 expression, and increased FOXP3+ proportions upon restimulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'the author's use of both Nrn1-/- T cells as well as anti-Nrn1 neutralizing Ab to achieve similar results is a strength,' explicitly affirming this complementary approach.

results.result: Nrn1-/- CD4 effector T cells show increased Ki67 expression and inflammatory cytokine production upon restimulation. In a Treg depletion model (FDG mice), Nrn1-/- mice showed accelerated weight loss and enhanced inflammatory T cell responses with increased Ki67 and cytokine expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'the in vivo functional studies of anergy development, Treg suppression, and EAE development are also well performed and strengthen the notion that Nrn1 is an important regulator of CD4 responsiveness.' This model is not specifically critiqued by reviewers.

results.result: Nrn1-/- effector T cells show enrichment of membrane repolarization gene sets, elevated Gria3 expression, comparable baseline membrane potential, enrichment of ion channel and amino acid transporter gene sets, and enhanced membrane potential changes in response to amino acid entry.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 acknowledges the data but emphasizes 'it remains unclear how Nrn1...suppresses the membrane potential and restrains aerobic glycolysis during Teff cell differentiation,' indicating the mechanism is not understood. Reviewer 2's concerns about biological replicates and statistical testing apply here as well.

results.result: Nrn1-/- effector T cells show enhanced mTOR and S6 phosphorylation, increased nutrient sensing, enrichment of glycolysis and proliferation gene sets, and confirmed increased glycolysis by seahorse assay while maintaining comparable oxygen consumption.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'Nrn1-/- Tregs and Teff cells each express a unique pattern of genes associated with...mTORC1 signaling activities, different than that seen in wild-type mice' but emphasizes the lack of mechanistic clarity. Reviewer 2's concerns about replicates and the use of multiple models without thorough mechanistic investigation apply.

results.result: Nrn1-/- mice show exacerbated EAE disease with increased severity, persistence, and weight loss, associated with increased immune cell infiltration in the spinal cord, increased MOG-specific CD4 cells, reduced FOXP3+ cells, and increased inflammatory cytokine-producing cells.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states 'the in vivo functional studies of anergy development, Treg suppression, and EAE development are also well performed and strengthen the notion that Nrn1 is an important regulator of CD4 responsiveness,' and notes 'with such defects in anergy induction as well as dysregulated Treg and Teff cell survival and function, auto reactive effector T cell activation becomes unrestrained and Nrn1-/- mice are more susceptible to severe EAE development.'

results.result: The overall conclusion that Nrn1 moderates T cell tolerance and immunity through context-dependent effects on Treg and effector T cells, impacting ion channel and nutrient transporter expression, metabolic states, and autoimmune disease progression.
results.evaluation: The editor/reviewer summary states 'these findings are solid and important for understanding immune regulation involving Treg cells and effector T cells,' but Reviewer 2 emphasizes 'multiple models have been used, but none has been studied thoroughly enough to provide really conclusive and unambiguous data' and 'in the absence of more in-depth study, the conclusions drawn by the authors are often open to questions.' Reviewer 3 notes 'the major weakness of this study stems from a lack of a clear molecular mechanism involving Nrn1.'

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate claims C9-C15 about Nrn1 expression in tolerance-associated T cell populations. OpenEval finds the data well-supported by qRT-PCR, western blot, and flow cytometry. Peer reviewers find the characterization 'comprehensive and convincing' but raise uncertainty about anti-Nrn1 antibody specificity, requesting validation using Nrn1 KO mice and suggesting addition of FACS data for single-cell quantitation.

Both evaluate claims C16-C21 about baseline phenotypic characterization of Nrn1-/- mice. OpenEval finds the data support no major developmental defects or spontaneous autoimmunity. Peer reviewers raise uncertainty about using Nrn1+/- and Nrn1+/+ cells interchangeably as controls, noting they may differ under activation/inflammatory conditions despite homeostatic similarity.

Both evaluate the peptide-induced anergy model (claims C22-C26). OpenEval finds the data comprehensively support defective anergy development in Nrn1-/- cells. Peer reviewers find the claims unsupported, stating 'the authors assume that this immunization protocol induces anergic cells, but they provide no experimental evidence' and noting that lack of IL-2 could reflect fewer OVA-specific cells rather than anergic status.

OpenEval R5 includes claim C27 about reduced early activation. Peer R4 evaluates only C27 and finds it supported, noting consistency with context-dependent effects and that 'naive cells lacking Nrn1 expression show normal electrical and metabolic behaviors.'

Both evaluate claims C28-C32 about iTreg differentiation and expansion. OpenEval finds the data support distinguishing between normal differentiation and impaired expansion. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, stating 'the use of iTregs to try to understand what is happening in vivo is problematic' as iTregs 'have probably no equivalent in vivo, and so may have no physiological relevance,' suggesting use of purified nTreg instead.

Both evaluate claims C33-C38 about in vivo Treg suppression assays. OpenEval finds the data consistently support reduced Treg suppressive capacity across multiple readouts. Peer reviewers find the claims unsupported, raising critical concerns that low FOXP3+ percentages (5-15%) may reflect Tconv contamination, and that 'higher tumor rejection could be due to an overactivation of Nrn1-/- Tconvs (rather than a defect in Nrn1-/- Treg function).'

Both evaluate RNASeq/GSEA and membrane potential findings in iTregs (claims C39-C42, C44-C47). OpenEval finds the connection between gene expression and cellular phenotype well-demonstrated. Peer reviewers acknowledge 'data shown here provide evidence for alterations in the electrical and metabolic state' but express uncertainty, emphasizing 'it remains unclear how Nrn1 reinforces the membrane potential and facilitates aerobic glycolysis.' Concerns about iTreg physiological relevance also apply.

Both evaluate metabolic and mTORC1 signaling claims (C48-C52). OpenEval finds the mechanistic link from nutrient transporter expression through mTORC1 to metabolic changes well-supported. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about the mechanism and raise concerns about small biological replicates ('RNAseq bulk data are based on biological duplicates') and iTreg relevance.

Both evaluate claims C53-C54 about naive T cells showing normal membrane potential and metabolism. OpenEval finds this critical control rules out developmental explanations. Peer reviewers explicitly support this finding, noting 'importantly, naive cells lacking Nrn1 expression show normal electrical and metabolic behaviors,' affirming context-dependent effects.

Both evaluate claims C55-C56 about antibody blocking experiments phenocopying genetic deletion. OpenEval finds this supports a functional rather than developmental role. Peer reviewers explicitly support this approach, noting 'the author's use of both Nrn1-/- T cells as well as anti-Nrn1 neutralizing Ab to achieve similar results is a strength.'

Both evaluate claims C57-C60 about enhanced Te cell responses. OpenEval finds consistent enhancement across multiple readouts with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers support these findings, stating 'the in vivo functional studies of anergy development, Treg suppression, and EAE development are also well performed and strengthen the notion that Nrn1 is an important regulator of CD4 responsiveness.'

Both evaluate claims C61-C65 about ion channel expression and membrane potential in Te cells. OpenEval finds the data show distinct functional consequences compared to iTregs. Peer reviewers acknowledge the data but express uncertainty, emphasizing 'it remains unclear how Nrn1...suppresses the membrane potential and restrains aerobic glycolysis during Teff cell differentiation,' indicating lack of mechanistic understanding.

Both evaluate claims C68-C71 about cell-context-dependent metabolic effects. OpenEval finds the data demonstrate opposite metabolic changes in Te cells versus iTregs. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, noting unique gene expression patterns but emphasizing lack of mechanistic clarity and concerns about replicates and use of multiple models without thorough mechanistic investigation.

OpenEval R14 includes claims C66-C67 about nutrient transporter expression and mTORC1 in Te cells. Peer R12 partially overlaps with these claims. Peer reviewers acknowledge the patterns but emphasize mechanistic uncertainty.

Both evaluate claims C72-C78 about EAE disease model. OpenEval finds comprehensive data showing consistent exacerbation across clinical and immunological parameters. Peer reviewers support these findings, stating 'the in vivo functional studies...are also well performed' and noting that 'with such defects in anergy induction as well as dysregulated Treg and Teff cell survival and function, auto reactive effector T cell activation becomes unrestrained and Nrn1-/- mice are more susceptible to severe EAE development.'

Both evaluate main conclusions (claims C109-C116) synthesizing all findings. OpenEval finds conclusions well-supported by comprehensive data showing opposite effects in Tregs versus Te cells. Peer reviewers express uncertainty: while acknowledging 'these findings are solid and important,' they emphasize 'multiple models have been used, but none has been studied thoroughly enough to provide really conclusive and unambiguous data' and note 'the major weakness of this study stems from a lack of a clear molecular mechanism involving Nrn1.'
